newsitem.title: ITALY: Papal assailant Agca agrees to Turkey extradition.
newsitem.headline: Papal assailant Agca agrees to Turkey extradition.

text.p: Mehmet Ali Agca, the Turk who shot Pope John Paul in 1981, has agreed to be extradited to his homeland, his lawyer said on Thursday.
Marina Magistrelli told Reuters by telephone from the central city of Ancona, near where Agca is serving a life sentence, that Turkey had renewed a request for his extradition recently.
Agca gave his formal consent to an Italian judicial official on Thursday morning.
Agca, who shot the Pope on May 13, 1981, is wanted in his native country for the killing of Turkish journalist Abdi Ipekci in 1978.

The move to send Agca back home came two weeks after the last remaining investigation into the Papal assassination attempt was closed for technical reasons and judicial sources said new inquiries could most likely not begin.
The possibility of extraditing Agca to Turkey had been complicated in the past because the country still practised capital punishment.
The Italian constitution does not allow convicts to be extradited to countries where capital punishment is practiced.
But an execution has not been carried out in Turkey since 1984 and Magistrelli said the death penalty there effectively "no longer exists".
Magistrelli said the plan, which would envisage Agca being granted a reprieve for the years remaining to be served in Italy, still had to be approved by the Italian justice minister.
Magistrelli said Agca would serve some 10 years in prison for the Ipekci murder if he returned home.

"This would be more like an act of clemency now," Magistrelli said, noting that 16 years of investigations had not been able to prove allegations that Agca had been part of a wider conspiracy to kill the Pope.

She said that the extradition would now be easier after the closing of the last investigation earlier this month, which centred on whether Agca was helped by a second gunman. That inquiry never made much headway.
The assassination attempt against the Pope is one of the enduring mysteries among the great crimes of the 20th century.
It has been the subject of three investigations and two trials.
Agca was arrested in St Peter's Square minutes after shooting the Pope. He underwent a first trial two months later and was handed down the life sentence that he is serving near Ancona.

At a second trial in 1986, prosecutors failed to prove their charges that the Bulgarian secret services had hired Agca on behalf of the Soviet Union in order to snuff out the Pope's support for the Solidarity union in his homeland.

At the time, Solidarity was threatening the stability of the Soviet bloc and the Pope reportedly told the late Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev that if Moscow invaded Poland he would support any resistance.
The so-called "Bulgarian Connection" trial ended with an "acquittal for lack of sufficient evidence" of three Turks and three Bulgarians charged with conspiring along with Agca.
